  "text": "The council sent a letter asking me to stop feeding the ducks.

I hadn't visited the pond in twenty years.

A photograph was enclosed. It showed an elderly woman on a bench, scattering breadcrumbs. She wore my coat. On the back, someone had written tomorrow's date.

I called the number at the bottom.

“It's a preventative notice,” the woman said.

“That's not me.”

“Not yet. Please stay away from the water.”

I burned the photograph in the sink.

The next morning, my coat pockets were full of bread.

I decided to take it to the council offices. Someone there could explain the letter, and I wanted them to see the pockets before I emptied them.

The building was boarded up.

Through a gap in the plywood, I could see a reception desk beneath a sheet of dust. A telephone rang behind it.

My mobile rang too.

“You should have stayed home,” the woman said.

Across the street, the park gates swung open.

I remembered then why I hadn't visited the pond. My mother had drowned there. They'd found her handbag on the bench, packed with bread she hadn't bought.

Something quacked behind me.

A duck stood on the pavement. Water dripped from its bill.

It opened its mouth.

“Darling,” my mother said. “You've kept me waiting.”

I backed against the boarded door. More ducks came through the gates, walking slowly, watching my hands.

The woman was still speaking through my phone.

“Keep your fists closed. If they see food, they'll call the others.”

My fingers were stiff. I looked down.

Both hands were wrinkled, spotted, and full of crumbs."
